title: The Water Keeps Rising
domain: Shipboard damage control and fluid systems
role: You are the damage-control assistant coordinating the casualty response.

intro.title: Read the whole flooding panel
intro.lead: A rising bilge alarm does not identify its source. Salinity, system pressure, isolation response, tank soundings, pump performance, and list reveal where the water comes from and whether the ship is gaining on it.

cards.title: How water enters
cards.body: Flooding can cross the hull boundary, escape from a pressurized seawater system, move through ballast piping, or only appear to rise because a sensor fails.

cards.title: How systems identify themselves
cards.body: A ruptured pressurized branch loses pressure. A ballast error changes tank inventory. A hull breach ignores isolation of intact ship systems.

cards.title: What dewatering proves
cards.body: Pump discharge confirms real water and establishes whether removal capacity exceeds the ingress rate.

cards.title: Why calm readings matter
cards.body: Normal firemain and cooling pressure can be decisive: they show which plausible seawater sources are not feeding the compartment.

intro.takeaway: Trace the water across boundaries. The correct diagnosis must explain its salinity, rate, pressure signature, valve response, and stability effect at the same time.

parts: Shell plating and sea chests separate the compartment from outside seawater.
A high-pressure seawater network supplies firefighting stations.
Sea-connected pumps and coolers remove heat from equipment.
Valves and tanks intentionally move seawater to control draft, list, and trim.
Level sensors and pumps detect and remove water from normally dry spaces.
system.soWrong: The same rising-level alarm can come from five different physical paths—or no water at all. Pressure, salinity, valve response, tank inventory, and independent level measurements locate the path.

level.name: Machinery-room bilge level
level.purpose: Shows water accumulation in the compartment; a rise may be real ingress or a bad channel.

salinity.name: Bilge conductivity / salinity
salinity.purpose: Distinguishes seawater-like ingress from fresh condensate or a dry sensor alarm.

firemain.name: Firemain pressure
firemain.purpose: Falls when a pressurized firemain branch ruptures or is isolated.

cooling.name: Seawater cooling pressure
cooling.purpose: Falls when the machinery cooling branch loses inventory or pump head.

isolation.name: Isolation response
isolation.purpose: Shows whether closing a named branch stops the ingress rate.

list.name: Ship list
list.purpose: A growing asymmetric flood adds off-center weight; a false level signal does not.

ballast.name: Ballast-tank soundings
ballast.purpose: Reveal commanded or accidental movement of seawater through the ballast system.

pump.name: Bilge-pump discharge
pump.purpose: Confirms whether the pump is moving water and whether ingress exceeds removal.

redundant.name: Independent level channel
redundant.purpose: Confirms a physical water rise independently of the presenting sensor.

adjacent.name: Adjacent compartment boundary
adjacent.purpose: Checks for progressive flooding beyond the initial watertight boundary.

hull.label: Hull breach below the waterline
hull.choice: Seawater enters directly through damaged shell plating and continues despite isolation of intact ship systems.

call.title: Hull breach — set boundaries and patch.
call.arg: Ingress is external to ship piping; control progressive flooding and establish a patch or shoring plan.

firemain.label: Ruptured firemain branch
firemain.choice: Pressurized seawater escapes from the firemain; branch isolation collapses the ingress rate.

call.title: Firemain rupture — isolate the branch.
call.arg: Secure the damaged firemain section while preserving alternate firefighting supply.

cooling.label: Seawater cooling-line rupture
cooling.choice: A machinery cooling branch loses pressure and spills seawater until its sea-connected valves are shut.

call.title: Cooling-line rupture — isolate and shift cooling.
call.arg: Secure the failed branch and protect affected machinery from loss of cooling.

ballastx.label: Uncommanded ballast transfer or overflow
ballastx.choice: A ballast valve lineup moves seawater into an unintended tank or overflow path, shifting list and tank soundings.

call.title: Ballast transfer — correct the valve lineup.
call.arg: Stop the uncommanded transfer and verify tank boundaries and vent paths.

sensor.label: Bilge-level sensor fault
sensor.choice: The presenting channel rises without physical water, conductivity, pump flow, list, or agreement from the redundant channel.

call.title: Sensor fault — verify locally and repair.
call.arg: Do not start flooding actions on a number that no independent measurement confirms.

pumpfail.label: Bilge-pump casualty with ordinary leakage
pumpfail.choice: Normal small leakage accumulates because the selected bilge pump is not producing discharge.

call.title: Bilge-pump casualty — shift pumps.
call.arg: Restore dewatering before routine leakage becomes a stability problem.

normal.label: Normal drain-down after maintenance
normal.choice: A known, finite maintenance drain produces a small temporary bilge rise that stops at the documented volume.

call.title: Documented drain-down — monitor.
call.arg: Keep dewatering available and verify the expected finite volume closes.

reassuring.note: The casualty is still contained to one compartment, but rising head can turn a local flood into progressive flooding.

poleA.note: Pressure collapses as the bilge begins rising.

rounds.hook: A sharp metallic report is followed by water spreading across the forward machinery-room deck. Both level channels rise together.
rounds.riddle: The water is salty and pressurized. Is it entering through the hull, the cooling plant, or the firemain?

isolation.observed: Ingress falls below 0.1 m³/min after frame-72 firemain isolation
isolation.reference: No change if source is hull

pump.observed: 18 m³/h discharge; level falling after isolation

reasons.hull: A hull breach shares salty rising water, but it would not collapse firemain pressure or stop when a firemain branch is isolated.
reasons.cooling: A cooling-line rupture shares salty water, but cooling pressure is steady while firemain pressure collapses.
reasons.ballastx: A ballast error should alter tank soundings and valve lineup; all tanks remain on plan.
reasons.sensor: Both level channels agree and the pump is discharging real water.
reasons.pumpfail: The pump is producing near-rated flow, so accumulation came from a source stronger than ordinary leakage.
reasons.normal: A planned drain would have a documented finite volume and would not depress the firemain.

resolve.title: Ruptured firemain branch
paras: Firemain pressure falls exactly as salty water appears, cooling pressure and ballast remain normal, and isolation of the local firemain branch stops the ingress.
The pump then gains on the remaining water, confirming that the source—not dewatering capacity—was the casualty.

why.loud: Why the loud reading works: only the firemain casualty combines compartment flooding with a large firemain-pressure loss.
why.quiet: Why the quiet readings confirm it: normal cooling pressure and tank soundings eliminate two other seawater systems, while branch isolation stops the source.

chain: Local isolation stops ingress and dewatering recovers
resolve.take: Use system pressure plus isolation response to trace flooding back to the pipe that supplied it.

logic: Hull, firemain, cooling, or ballast source remains
Firemain rupture becomes the direct system explanation
Cooling pressure and ballast soundings normal

poleA.note: Pressure falls only on the port seawater-cooling loop.

rounds.hook: During a high-load engineering watch, water begins spraying from behind a machinery skid. Firemain pressure remains normal.
rounds.riddle: The bilge rise is real and salty. Which sea-connected system is losing pressure, and does isolating it stop the leak?

isolation.observed: Spray stops after port cooler inlet and outlet shut

reasons.hull: A hull breach would continue after closing the cooler inlet and outlet; here the spray stops.
reasons.firemain: Firemain pressure is normal and firemain isolation is not what changed the leak.
reasons.ballastx: No ballast tank or valve position changes accompany the event.
reasons.sensor: Two level channels, salty conductivity, visible spray, and pump discharge confirm real water.
reasons.pumpfail: The pump is producing near-rated flow; the problem is a pressurized source, not failed dewatering.
reasons.normal: A maintenance drain is not a high-pressure spray and would be documented and finite.

resolve.title: Ruptured seawater-cooling branch
paras: Only the port cooling loop loses pressure. The firemain and ballast system stay normal, and closing both sides of the cooler branch stops the spray.
Because the source is isolated and the bilge pump is healthy, the water level begins to fall without progressive flooding.

why.loud: Why the loud reading works: the affected cooling loop loses pressure while the other seawater systems remain steady.
why.quiet: Why the quiet readings confirm it: two-sided branch isolation stops the leak, proving the source lies inside that piping boundary.

chain: Sea-connected loop sprays into machinery room
Inlet and outlet isolation stop the source
resolve.take: A pressure loss identifies the candidate system; an isolation test proves the boundary.

logic: Hull, firemain, cooling, or ballast source remains
Cooling pressure low while firemain normal

poleA.val: 0.9 m³/min after all local systems isolated
poleA.note: Water continues to enter from low on the shell side.

rounds.hook: After a collision with floating debris, a low compartment reports rapid flooding. All local seawater piping can be isolated, but the level keeps climbing.
rounds.riddle: Every ship system now reads normal. Does continuing seawater ingress prove the source is outside the piping system?

isolation.observed: No rate change after firemain, cooling, and ballast isolation
isolation.reference: A piping source should slow or stop

reasons.firemain: A firemain source should lower firemain pressure and respond to branch isolation; neither occurs.
reasons.cooling: Cooling pressure is normal and cooling isolation does not change the rate.
reasons.ballastx: Tank soundings remain fixed and ballast isolation does not change ingress.
reasons.sensor: Independent level, salinity, list, and pump discharge all prove physical water.
reasons.pumpfail: The pump is at rated discharge; it is simply smaller than the measured ingress.
reasons.normal: A documented drain cannot sustain a 54 m³/h rate or produce increasing list after all system isolation.

resolve.title: Hull breach below the waterline
paras: Seawater continues entering at roughly 54 m³/h after every local sea-connected piping system is isolated. System pressures and tank soundings remain normal, so the source lies outside those networks.
The bilge pump is healthy but undersized for the casualty. Increasing list and independent level agreement show a growing off-center flood that requires patching, shoring, and boundary control.

why.loud: Why the loud readings tie: several casualties can produce salty water and a rising bilge.
why.quiet: Why the quiet readings decide it: normal system pressures plus no response to isolation remove every internal seawater path, leaving the shell boundary.

chain: Shell plating is opened below the waterline
External sea pressure drives continuous ingress
Pumping cannot keep up until the hull opening is controlled
resolve.take: When every internal source is isolated and the rate persists, move the causal boundary outward to the hull.

logic: No change after all system isolation
